title: 1  L29: 9.1 Higher-Order Linear Equations.
text:
NoteDefinition



A differential operator \(L\) is linear iff for any two functions \(y_1\) and \(y_2\)
\[L[c_1y_1+c_2y_2]=c_1L[y_1]+c_2L[y_2]\]

title: 1  L29: 9.1 Higher-Order Linear Equations.
text:
1.2 Example 1






TipExample



Let \[ L = 3\frac{d}{dx}+2\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\]






CautionSolution





\[L[c_1y_1+c_2y_2]=\left(3\frac{d}{dx}+2\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\right)\left(c_1y_1+c_2y_2\right)\] \[=c_1\left(3\frac{d}{dx}+2\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\right) y_1+c_2\left(3\frac{d}{dx}+2\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\right) y_2\] \[=c_1L[y_1]+c_2L[y_2]\]

title: 1  L29: 9.1 Higher-Order Linear Equations.
text:
1.3 Theorem for higher order






NoteTheorem




Theorem 1.1 If \(a_n(x),a_{n-1}(x),\cdots,a_0(x)\) are continuous over the interval \(I\), and if \(a_n(x)\neq 0\) then \[L[y]=0 \tag{1.1}\] where \[L=a_n(x)\frac{d^n}{dx^n}+\cdots+a_1(x)\frac{d}{dx}+a_0(x)\] has \(n\) linearly independent solutions \[y_1(x),\cdots,y_n(x)\] Furthermore if \(y(x)\) is any solution to Equation 1.1 then \(\exists \, c_1,c_2,\cdots,c_n\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[y(x)=c_1y_1+c_2y_2+\cdots +c_ny_n\]

title: 1  L29: 9.1 Higher-Order Linear Equations.
text:
1.4 Wronskian






NoteDefinition



The Wronskian of a set of functions \[f_1(x),f_2(x),\cdots,f_n(x)\] is equal to the determinant
\[\begin{vmatrix} f_1(x) & f_2(x) &\dots & f_n(x)\\ f_1'(x) & \ddots && \vdots\\
\vdots &&\ddots&\vdots\\
f_1^{(n-1)}(x) & f_2^{(n-1)}(x) &\dots & f_n^{(n-1)}(x)
\end{vmatrix}\]
and is denoted by \(W[f_1(x),\cdots,f_n(x)]\)

title: 1  L29: 9.1 Higher-Order Linear Equations.
text:
1.5 Theorem for Wronskian






NoteTheorem




Theorem 1.2 \(\{f_1(x),f_2(x),\cdots,f_n(x)\}\) are linearly independent on \(I\) iff \[W[f_1(x),\cdots,f_n(x)]\neq 0\]

1.8 STHOLH/ODES/WCC






NoteDefinition



Solutions to higher order Linear Homogeneous ODES1 with constant coefficients
\[a_{n}y^{(n)}+a_{n-1}y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+a_1y'+a_0y=0 \tag{1.2}\]
Characteristic Equation:
\[a_nr^n+a_{n-1}r^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1r+a_0=0 \tag{1.3}\]
has \(n\) solutions.

1.9 Distinct real roots
If \(r_1,\cdots,r_k\), with \(k\leq n\), are distinct real roots of Equation 1.3 then
\[y=c_1e^{r_1x}+c_2e^{r_2x}+\cdots+c_ke^{r_kx}\] is a solution to Equation 1.2


1.10 Complex real roots
If \(\alpha_1\pm i\beta_1,\quad\alpha_2\pm i\beta_2,\quad\cdots\quad,\alpha_k\pm i\beta_k\), are roots of Equation 1.3 with \(k\leq \frac{n}{2}\). Then \[y=e^{\alpha_1x}(c_{11}\cos\beta_1x+c_{12}\sin\beta_1x)\] \[+e^{\alpha_2x}(c_{21}\cos\beta_2x+c_{22}\sin\beta_2x)\] \[+\cdots+e^{\alpha_kx}(c_{k1}\cos\beta_kx+c_{k2}\sin\beta_kx)\] is a solution to Equation 1.2


1.11 Repeated real roots
If \(r=m\) is a \(k\) repeated root of Equation 1.2, with \(k\leq n\), Then
\[y=c_1e^{mx}+c_2xe^{mx}+c_3x^2e^{mx}\cdots+c_kx^{k-1}e^{mx}\] is a solution to Equation 1.3

text:
1.12 Example 4






TipExample



Solve:
\[y^{(5)}+3y^{(3)}-4y'=0\]






CautionSolution





Characteristic eq\(^n\):
\[r^5+3r^3-4r=0\] \[r(r^4+3r^2-4)=0\]
Let \(u=r^2\) \(\rightarrow (r^4+3r^2-4)=(u^2+3u-4)=(u-1)(u+4)\)
\[\Rightarrow r(r^2-1)(r^2+4)=0\]
\[r(r+1)(r-1)(r+2i)(r-2i)=0\]
\[r_{oots}=0,-1,1,-2i,2i,\] \[\boxed{y=c_1+c_2e^{-x}+c_3e^x+c_4\cos 2x+c_5\sin 2x}\] is the general solution.

3 Intro
A system of differential equations consists of multiple differential equations that involve the same set of variables and their derivatives. These systems are commonly used to model situations where multiple related quantities change with respect to one another, typically over time. The variables can represent different physical quantities, like position, velocity, temperature, or chemical concentrations, depending on the context of the problem.
There are two main types of systems of differential equations:
Systems of differential equations can be linear or nonlinear, and they can be solved using various methods, depending on their complexity and the characteristics of the equations involved. Analytical solutions are available for simpler systems, while numerical methods might be necessary for more complex or nonlinear systems.

3.1 Wronskian to test if vectors solutions are independent






NoteDefinition



place each vector solution in each column, then calculate the determinant of the matrix
\[\det(W)=\begin{vmatrix}
a & b & c \\
d & e & f \\
g & h & i \\
\end{vmatrix}
\]
if \(\det(W)\neq 0\), then solutions are independent of each other



3.1.1 Example






TipExample



Test if \(y_1, y_2,\text{ and }y_3\) are independent solutions:

Vector Solution \(\mathbf{y}_1(t)\): \[
\mathbf{y}_1(t) = \begin{bmatrix} e^t \\ t^2 \\ \sin(t) \end{bmatrix}
\]
Vector Solution \(\mathbf{y}_2(t)\): \[
\mathbf{y}_2(t) = \begin{bmatrix} t e^t \\ 1 \\ \cos(t) \end{bmatrix}
\]
Vector Solution \(\mathbf{y}_3(t)\): \[
\mathbf{y}_3(t) = \begin{bmatrix} e^{-t} \\ t \\ t \sin(t) \end{bmatrix}
\]







CautionSolution





\[
W(t) =
\begin{bmatrix}
e^t     & t e^t & e^{-t} \\
t^2     & 1     & t      \\
\sin(t) & \cos(t) & t\sin(t)
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[\cdots\]

title: 2  L30: 10.4 Distinct Eigenvalues
text:
4.1 Example 1:






TipExample



\[\frac{dx}{dt}=x-y\]
\[\frac{dy}{dt}=2x+4y\]






CautionSolution






4.1.1 Step 1:(eigenvalues)
\[\begin{vmatrix}
a-\lambda & b\\
c & d-\lambda
\end{vmatrix}\Rightarrow\begin{vmatrix}
1-\lambda & -1\\
2 & 4-\lambda
\end{vmatrix} =0\]
\[\lambda^2-5\lambda+6=0\]
\[(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)=0\] \[\lambda_{1,2}= \{2,3\}\]


4.1.2 Step 2:(eigenvectors)

\(\boxed{\lambda=2}\)
\[\begin{bmatrix}
1-2 & -1\\
2 & 4-2
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=0\]
\[\Rightarrow\begin{bmatrix}
-1 & -1\\
2& 2
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=0\]
\[-k_1-k_2=0\]
pick \(k_1=1\) \(\Rightarrow k_2=-1\) (\(k_1\) arbitrary)
Eigenvector: \(\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}\)

\(\boxed{\lambda=3}\)
\[\begin{bmatrix}
1-3 & -1\\
2 & 4-3
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=0\]
\[\Rightarrow\begin{bmatrix}
-2 & -1\\
2& 1
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=0\]
\[\Rightarrow 2k_1+k_2=0\Rightarrow k_1=1\Rightarrow k_2=-2\] Eigenvector: \(\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}\)


4.1.3 Step 3:(general solution)

\[\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}c_1e^{2t}+\begin{bmatrix}1\\-2\end{bmatrix}c_2e^{3t}\]


OR
\[x(t)=c_1e^{2t}+c_2e^{3t}\] \[y(t)=-c_1e^{2t}-2c_2e^{3t}\]

title: 2  L30: 10.4 Distinct Eigenvalues
text:
4.2 Example 2






TipExample



\[\frac{dx}{dt}=3x\]
\[\frac{dy}{dt}=2x-y\]






CautionSolution






Step 1(eigenvalues):

\[\begin{vmatrix}
3-\lambda & 0\\
2 & -1-\lambda
\end{vmatrix}=0\]
\[(3-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-0=0\] \[(\lambda-3)(\lambda+1)=0\] \[\boxed{\lambda=3},\quad \boxed{\lambda=-1}\]


Step 2(eigenvector 1):

\(\boxed{\lambda=3}\)

\[\begin{bmatrix}
3-3 & 0\\
2 & -1-3
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}\]


\[2k_1-4k_2=0\] \[k_1-2k_2=0\] \[k_1=2k_2\]


Eigenvector 1: \(\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}\)


Step 2(eigenvector 2):
\(\boxed{\lambda=-1}\)
\[\begin{bmatrix}
3-^-1 & 0\\
2 & -1-^-1
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[4k_1+0=0\rightarrow k_1=0\rightarrow k_2=\text{my choice}=1\]
Eigenvector 2: \(\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\)


Step 3(general solution):


\[\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}c_1e^{3t}+\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}c_2e^{-t}\]



4.3 Using R

A <- matrix(c(3, 0, 2, -1), 2, 2, byrow=TRUE)
A

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    3    0
[2,]    2   -1

eigen(A)

eigen() decomposition
$values
[1]  3 -1

$vectors
          [,1] [,2]
[1,] 0.8944272    0
[2,] 0.4472136    1


Each column are the normalized eigenvectors, i.e
\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^2+1^2}}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0.8944272\\0.4472136\end{bmatrix}\]

title: 2  L30: 10.4 Distinct Eigenvalues
text:
4.4 Example 3






TipExample



Find the general solution of
\[{\bf y}'=\left[\begin{array}{rrr}3&-1&-1\\-2& 3& 2\\4&-1&-2\end{array}\right]{\bf y}\]






CautionSolution





\[\left|\begin{array}{ccc}3-\lambda&-1&-1\\-2&3-\lambda& 2\\4 &-1&-2-\lambda\end{array}\right|=-(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)(\lambda+1).\nonumber\]






CautionNarrative:





Solving a \(3 \times 3\) system of linear differential equations often involves a methodical approach that can be extended from methods used in smaller systems. Here’s a step-by-step explanation of the typical methods used, primarily focusing on homogeneous systems:

4.4.1 1. Write the System in Matrix Form
First, express the system of differential equations in matrix form. Suppose we have: \[\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = A \mathbf{x}\] where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the vector of variables, and \(A\) is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix containing the coefficients of the system.


4.4.2 2. Find the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
The next step is to solve the characteristic equation of the matrix \(A\), which is given by: \[\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\] where \(\lambda\) is a scalar (the eigenvalue), and \(I\) is the \(3 \times 3\) identity matrix. This will yield a cubic equation in \(\lambda\), solving which gives us the eigenvalues.


4.4.3 3. Compute the Eigenvectors
For each eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\), find the corresponding eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}_i\) by solving: \[(A - \lambda_i I) \mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0}\] This system of equations may sometimes need to be solved using methods like Gaussian elimination.


4.4.4 4. Form the General Solution
If the eigenvalues are distinct, the general solution to the differential equation can be expressed as: \[\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1 e^{\lambda_1 t} \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t} \mathbf{v}_2 + c_3 e^{\lambda_3 t} \mathbf{v}_3\] where \(c_1, c_2,\) and \(c_3\) are constants determined by the initial conditions.


4.4.5 5. Handle Special Cases

Repeated Eigenvalues: If any eigenvalue is repeated, you may need to find generalized eigenvectors to form a complete set of solutions.

Complex Eigenvalues: If the eigenvalues are complex, the solution will involve trigonometric functions (sines and cosines) and possibly exponential functions, reflecting oscillatory behavior.



4.4.6 6. Use Initial Conditions
Finally, use the initial conditions provided to solve for the constants \(c_1, c_2,\) and \(c_3\).
This approach will allow you to solve any \(3 \times 3\) system of linear differential equations, assuming it can be described by constant coefficients and is homogeneous. Non-homogeneous systems (i.e., systems with a non-zero right-hand side) would typically require additional steps such as finding a particular solution.

title: 3  L31: 10.6 Complex Eigenvalues.
text:
Note




Theorem 3.1 (Theorem) Let \(\lambda=\alpha+i\beta,\qquad \beta>0\)
Let \(K\) be eigenvector associated with \(\lambda\)
\[K=\begin{bmatrix}u_1+iv_1\\u_2+iv_2\end{bmatrix}\]
Then \[x_1=e^{\alpha t}(B_1\cos \beta t +B_2\sin \beta t)\]
\[x_2=e^{\alpha t}(B_2\cos \beta t -B_1\sin \beta t)\]
is a fundamental set of real solution to our \(2\times 2\) system, where:
\[B_1=\begin{bmatrix}u_1\\u_2\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_2=-\begin{bmatrix}v_1\\v_2\end{bmatrix}\]




3.1.1 Example 1:






TipExample



\[\frac{dx}{dt}=3x-y\]
\[\frac{dy}{dt}=x+3y\]






CautionSolution






Step 1:(eigenvalues)
\[\begin{vmatrix}
3-\lambda & -1\\
1 & 3-\lambda
\end{vmatrix} =0\]
\[\lambda^2-6\lambda+10=0\]
\[\lambda=\frac{6\pm \sqrt{36-40}}{2}\] \[=\frac{6\pm \sqrt{-4}}{2}=\frac{6\pm 2\sqrt{-1} }{2}=\boxed{3\pm i}\]
Step 2:(eigenvector K)
\(\boxed{\lambda=(3+i)}\)
\[\begin{bmatrix}
3-(3+i) & -1\\
1 & 3-(3+i)
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[k_1-ik_2=0\] \[k_1=ik_2\]
\[\Rightarrow K= \begin{bmatrix}i\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0+1i\\1+0i\end{bmatrix}\]
\[\Rightarrow B_1=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_2=-\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\end{bmatrix}\] Step 3:(Fundamental set)
\[\vec{x_1}=e^{3t}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\cos t+\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\end{bmatrix}\sin t\right)\] and
\[\vec{x_2}=e^{3t}\left(\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\end{bmatrix}\cos t-\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\sin t\right)\]
and the general solution will be the linear combination of the fundamental set of real solutions.







3.1.2 Example 2:






TipExample



Find the general solution of
\[\frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}=\begin{bmatrix}4&-5\\5&-2\end{bmatrix}\vec{r}\]






CautionSolution





\[\begin{bmatrix}x'\\y'\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4&-5\\5&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}\]

3.1.3 Eigenvalues
\[\begin{vmatrix}4-\lambda & -5\\ 5& -2-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=0\]
\[\lambda^2-2\lambda+17=0\] \[\lambda=\frac{+2-\sqrt{4-4\cdot 17}}{2}\]
\[\lambda=\frac{+2-\sqrt{-4\cdot 16}}{2} = 1\pm 4i\]


3.1.4 Eigenvectors
Different representation, same method:
\(\boxed{\lambda = 1+ 4i}\)
\[\begin{bmatrix}4-(1+ 4i) & -5 &\vdots&0\\ 5& -2-(1+ 4i)&\vdots&0\end{bmatrix}\] \[\begin{bmatrix}3-4i & -5 &\vdots&0\\ 5& -3-4i&\vdots&0\end{bmatrix}\] \[(3-4i)k_1-5k_2=0\]

\[\frac{(3-4i)}{5}k_1=k_2\]
We choose \[k_1=5 \rightarrow k_2=3-4i\]
\[\Rightarrow{K=\begin{bmatrix}5\\3-4i\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5+0i\\3-4i\end{bmatrix}}\]
\[\Rightarrow B_1=\begin{bmatrix}5\\3\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_2=-\begin{bmatrix}0\\-4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\4\end{bmatrix}\]


3.1.5 Fundamental set
Then \[\vec{x_1}=e^{\alpha t}(B_1\cos \beta t +B_2\sin \beta t)\]
\[\vec{x_1}=e^{t}\left(\begin{bmatrix}5\\3\end{bmatrix}\cos 4 t +\begin{bmatrix}0\\4\end{bmatrix}\sin 4 t\right)\]
\[\vec{x_2}=e^{\alpha t}(B_2\cos \beta t -B_1\sin \beta t)\] \[\vec{x_2}=e^{t}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0\\4\end{bmatrix}\cos 4 t +\begin{bmatrix}-5\\-3\end{bmatrix}\sin 4 t\right)\]

[1,] 0.4242641+0.5656854i 0.4242641-0.5656854i
[2,] 0.7071068+0.0000000i 0.7071068+0.0000000i








CautionCode description





These code initializes a matrix named A. Here’s a breakdown of what each part of the function does:

matrix(): This is the function used in R to create a matrix. A matrix is a two-dimensional array of numbers.
c(4, -5, 5, -2): This is a vector containing the elements that will be filled into the matrix. The elements are 4, -5, 5, and -2.
2, 2: These numbers define the dimensions of the matrix. The first number (2) is the number of rows, and the second number (2) is the number of columns. So, this matrix will be a 2x2 matrix.
byrow=TRUE: This argument specifies how the matrix is filled with the elements from the vector. If byrow=TRUE, the matrix is filled row-wise from the vector. This means that the first two elements of the vector (4 and -5) will make up the first row of the matrix, and the next two elements (5 and -2) will make up the second row.

Therefore, the resulting matrix A will look like this:
\[
\begin{matrix}
4 & -5 \\
5 & -2 \\
\end{matrix}
\]
This matrix is stored in the variable A.

CautionR-script with initial conditions

To create an R script that computes the general solution of a system of linear differential equations using eigenvalues and eigenvectors. This code will compute the solution given initial conditions and will be useful for simulation or analysis purposes.

3.8.1 R Script Overview

Define the matrix ( A ).
Calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors using eigen().
Create a function to calculate ( x(t) ) at any given time ( t ) based on initial conditions ( x(0) ).



3.8.2 Step-by-Step R Code

# Load ggplot2 for plotting
library(ggplot2)

# Define the matrix A
A <- matrix(c(4, -5, 5, -2), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)

# Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors
eig <- eigen(A)

# Eigenvalues
lambdas <- eig$values

# Eigenvectors
vectors <- eig$vectors

# Function to compute x(t) for given initial conditions and time t
compute_xt <- function(t, initial_conditions) {
  # Ensure the initial_conditions is a matrix
  initial_conditions <- matrix(initial_conditions, nrow = 2)
  
  # Constants c1 and c2 from initial conditions, solving the linear system
  # vectors %*% c = initial_conditions
  # c is the vector of coefficients [c1; c2]
  coefficients <- solve(vectors, initial_conditions)
  
  # Compute x(t) = c1 * exp(lambda1 * t) * vector1 + c2 * exp(lambda2 * t) * vector2
  xt <- vectors %*% (coefficients * exp(lambdas * t))
  
  # Return the computed x(t) considering only the real parts
  return(Re(xt))
}

# Time range from 0 to 10, computing at intervals of 0.1
time_points <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1)
initial_conditions <- c(1, 0)

# Compute x(t) for each time point
results <- sapply(time_points, function(t) compute_xt(t, initial_conditions))

# Prepare data for plotting
data_frame <- data.frame(
  Time = rep(time_points, each = 2),
  X_t = c(results[1,], results[2,]),
  Component = rep(c("x1", "x2"), each = length(time_points))
)

# Plot using ggplot2
plot <- ggplot(data_frame, aes(x = Time, y = X_t, color = Component)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Components of x(t) over Time",
       x = "Time t",
       y = "Value of x(t)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red"))

# Print the plot
print(plot)














CautionCode Description






Matrix and Eigen Calculations: The matrix \(A\) is defined, and its eigenvalues and eigenvectors are computed.

Function compute_xt: This function calculates the solution \(x(t)\). It takes time \(t\) and initial conditions as arguments.

It first solves the equation \(Vc = x(0)\) for the coefficients vector \(c\) where \(V\) is the matrix of eigenvectors. The solve() function is used for solving linear systems.

It then calculates \(x(t) = V (c \cdot \exp(\lambda t))\), where \(\exp(\lambda t)\) applies the exponential function to each eigenvalue multiplied by \(t\), and \(c\) is multiplied element-wise.


Example Usage: The function is then used to compute \(x(t)\) for a specific set of initial conditions at \(t = 1\).

This script allows you to plug in any initial conditions and any time \(t\) to see the behavior of the system at that point.

title: 4  L32: 10.4 Repeated EigenValues.
text:
Note




Theorem 4.1 (Theorem) Suppose \(\lambda\) is a repeated eigenvalue for the system:
\[\frac{dx}{dt}=ax+by\] \[\frac{dy}{dt}=cx+dy\]
with eigenvector \(K\), then
\[\vec{x_1} = Ke^{\lambda t}\] \[\vec{x_2} = K\,t\,e^{\lambda t}+Pe^{\lambda t}\] Where \(P\) is to be determined from
\[\begin{bmatrix}a-\lambda & b\\ c& d-\lambda\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p_1\\p_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}\] is a fundamental set.




4.1.1 Example 1:






TipExample



Find the general solution to
\[\frac{dx}{dt}=4x-y\] \[\frac{dy}{dt}=x+2y\]






CautionSolution






4.1.2 eigenvalues:
\[\begin{bmatrix}4-\lambda & -1\\ 1& 2-\lambda\end{bmatrix}=0\]
\[(4-\lambda)(2-\lambda)+1=0\]
\[8-6\lambda+\lambda^2+1=0\] \[\lambda^2-6\lambda+9=0\] \[(\lambda-3)^2=0\]


4.1.3 eigenvectors:
\(\boxed{\lambda =3}:\)
\[\begin{bmatrix}4-3 & -1\\ 1& 2-3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[k_1-k_2=0\] \[k_1=k_2\] \[K=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\]


4.1.4 Fundamental set:
\(\vec{x_1}\) is done:
\[\vec{x_1}=Ke^{\lambda t}= \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}e^{3t} \] for \(\vec{x_2}\) we need to solve:
\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\ 1& -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p_1\\p_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}\] \[\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\ 1& -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p_1\\p_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\] \[p_1-p_2=1\] \[p_1=1+p_2\] \[P=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}\]
Therefore:
\[\vec{x_2}=e^{3t}\,t\,\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}+e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}\]


4.1.5 General Solution:
\[\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=c_1e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}+c_2\left(t\,e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}+e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}\right)\]








4.1.6 Example 2:






TipExample



\[\frac{dx}{dt}=y\] \[\frac{dy}{dt}=-9x+6y\]






CautionSolution





\[\begin{vmatrix}0-\lambda & 1\\ -9&6-\lambda\end{vmatrix}\]
\[-6\lambda+\lambda^2+9=0\] \[(\lambda-3)^2=0\]
\[\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1\\ -9& 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}k_1\\k_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[-3k_1+k_2=0\] \[K=\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[\vec{x_1}=Ke^{\lambda t}= e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix}\]
\[\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1\\ -9& 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p_1\\p_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix}\] \[-3p_1+p_2=1\] \[p_2=1+3p_1\] \[P=\begin{bmatrix}1\\4\end{bmatrix}\]
\[\vec{x_2}=t\,e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix}+e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\4\end{bmatrix}\]
Then the general solution is:
\[\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=c_1e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix}+c_2\left(t\,e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix}+e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\4\end{bmatrix}\right)\]
